claims.text: The starting material is a pressurelessly infiltrated W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix and no interfacial treatment.
All exposed W surfaces will be coated with an approximately 100 nm nanocrystalline Ni layer by electrodeposition before Cu infiltration.
The Ni-coated composite will undergo liquid-phase sintering at 1000–1050 °C under ambient pressure.
The Ni interlayer and subsequent processing will produce a continuous, approximately 200 nm thick graded W–Ni–Cu diffusion zone.
The graded interfacial zone will be enriched in Ni.
W–Ni and Ni–Cu solid solutions will form in the interfacial diffusion zone.
The Ni interlayer will lower W–Cu interfacial energy.
The Ni-containing graded zone will mitigate thermal-expansion mismatch at the W–Cu interface.
The graded zone will act as a diffusion bridge that suppresses Kirkendall void formation during irradiation and thermal cycling.
The Ni interlayer will suppress or prevent interfacial phase separation under high heat flux and irradiation.
After the specified service exposure, the Ni-treated composite will have at least 10% higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
After the specified service exposure, the Ni-treated composite will have at least 50% lower interfacial void volume fraction than the untreated composite.
The untreated W–Cu composite has an effective thermal conductivity of approximately 150 W/m·K after identical service exposure.
The untreated W–Cu composite has an interfacial void volume fraction of approximately 5% after identical service exposure.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at heat fluxes up to 2 MW/m² and service temperatures of 400–700 °C.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at neutron fluences up to 1×10²² n/m² for neutron energies above 0.1 MeV.
The claimed effect is bounded to Ni interlayer thicknesses between 50 and 200 nm.
Ni deposition quality and interdiffusion kinetics may cause variability in the proposed effect.
